issues.legal_issue: The post-amendment due-diligence condition for amending pleadings does not apply to a pleading filed before the amended pleading rules came into force.
material_facts: The suit was filed in 1998, before the 2002 amendments came into force.
An application to amend the plaint was made during the appeals, and the appellate court allowed it.
The High Court set aside that order by applying the proviso requiring a showing of due diligence.
issues.conclusion: The proviso did not apply to the suit because the pleading had been filed before the amended rules came into force. The High Court erred in relying on the proviso; its judgment was set aside and the matter remitted for fresh consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as amended, added a due-diligence condition for applications made after trial commenced. However, Section 16(2)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2002 provides that the amended pleading rules do not apply to pleadings filed before the relevant amendments came into force. The filing of the suit before that commencement therefore made the proviso inapplicable.

predicates.civil_suit_with_amendment_request: A party in a civil suit sought permission to amend a pleading.
predicates.pleading_filed_before_amended_rules_comm: The pleading in the suit was filed before the amended pleading rules came into force.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to amend a pleading in a civil suit and the pleading was filed before the amended rules commenced, the due-diligence requirement does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in seeking a pleading amendment, or the possibility that a fresh claim would be time-barred, does not remove the court’s power to allow amendment, though limitation and prejudice are relevant to its discretion.
material_facts: The application to amend the plaint was made during the appeals and was challenged as belated.
The respondent did not claim that the amendment made available relief that would otherwise have been barred by limitation.
The High Court set aside the amendment order based on the proviso, and the Supreme Court remitted the matter for fresh consideration with all contentions open.
issues.conclusion: Delay or laches is distinct from prejudice, and limitation is a relevant factor in deciding whether to allow an amendment but does not eliminate the court’s power to do so. The Supreme Court did not decide whether the amendment should ultimately be allowed; that question remained open on remand.
issues.legal_principle: Under L.J. Leach and Company Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co. and Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil, amendments should be assessed by whether they are necessary to determine the real controversy and whether they cause injustice that cannot be compensated in costs. A claim that would be time-barred in a fresh suit is a relevant discretionary consideration, not a limit on the court’s power. The Court also referred to Rajesh Kumar Aggarwal v. K.K. Modi, Pankaja v. Yellappa, Baldev Singh v. Manohar Singh, Gajanan Jaikishan Joshi v. Prabhakar Mohanlal Kalwar, and A.K. Gupta and Sons v. Damodar Valley Corporation.

predicates.civil_pleading_amendment_request: A party in a civil proceeding requested permission to amend a pleading.
predicates.application_is_delayed: The amendment request was made after delay or laches.
predicates.fresh_claim_would_be_time_barred: A fresh suit on the claim in the proposed amendment would be barred by limitation.

issues.definition: For a civil pleading amendment request, delay or a time-barred fresh claim does not by itself remove the court’s discretion to allow the amendment.
